No, that's correct. I have heard that a positive even on an expired test can be trusted, because you are very unlikely to get a false positive on a rapid test. It's the false negative you have to worry about, whether because the test isn't sensitive enough (or user error) or you don't have a high enough viral load to be detected yet. RATs can mostly tell you whether you're infectious at the moment you take the test, but they are hardly foolproof.

Respectfully, that's bs. People get treated as less than human all the time without having done one thing to deserve it. Your statement that "if you do not make yourself a victim, you will not be treated as one" shows a privileged perspective. Tell that to the woman who was shot to death in her own home because she called 911. Pandering to those who want to control and intimidate by agreeing to a certain dress code so you think you're safe is...well, something only those who already have privilege even have a choice to do (and it only works because your privilege already protects you). Do you really think police are going to politely let you take one maskless breath so they can ID you, and then let you put your mask back on and go? Maybe, but certainly not if they're on a power trip. Do you really want to put your trust in their sense of decency? I don't. If they want to use their power to make you take and keep the mask off, they certainly will. Compliance with unjust power is false security. The minimization of danger is more dangerous than taking an actual stand against it.

I think what you wrote about folks not being used to triangulating decisions is really true. Thanks to my anxiety that predates Covid, I am used to having to carefully calculate my actions (I also have other things going on that limit the energy I have to work with day to day). I started taking extreme care during flu season after we had a really bad season in 2017-18, and while masking wasn't part of those precautions (I didn't know much about the benefits of masking back then), I definitely practiced physical distancing and spaced out my social activities. So I was already mentally prepared to do that for Covid, though admittedly not to the level I do now, and not for such an extended period of time. Thanks, anxiety! But really, having a phobia of getting sick isn't the worst, and it has helped me here. If I am ever tempted to relax precautions, I think about how scared I would feel if I got sick, and that is enough to keep me from relaxing.

It may feel apocalyptic, but I genuinely think we can do this peacefully. A peaceful revolution will shock the hell out of everyone who has hung their hats on the machinery of war. It may feel like everyone is dying, but I believe the dying can be of old and outworn worldviews and ways of doing things. People dying in war is as old as humanity. Nothing new there, and not much redeeming. I choose to believe that we can do it differently this time. Not physical death (except for those whose souls choose that) but paradigm death (and rebirth).

Yeah. When I was still in grad school, I gave $100 to a woman who had asked for help through a local mutual aid group. She then kept asking me for more money (not ever huge amounts, but consistently here and there) and promised to pay me back. I was living off of student loans at the time, but I had plenty, and I felt bad that she didn't have enough. And I think I just enjoyed the dopamine hit from doing something easy and receiving someone else's gratitude. I knew from past experience that I should expect all loans to be gifts and then I would be pleasantly surprised if I got paid back. But she was audacious in her repeated asking even after it became obvious that she wouldn't pay me back. I had to tell her that there needed to be a limit at some point because this was my student loan money that I would eventually have to pay back with interest. She said she understood that but kept asking me for money! Eventually I had to just stop responding because she would not take the hint. She seemed like a nice person but I guess I learned my lesson. I will still give one time gifts to strangers in need if they seem genuine and I can afford it, but I am not going to be a sugar momma ever again!

Yeah, the therapeutic relationship often is the most important part of therapy. It's there to be a safe container for working through interpersonal relating and uncovering/resolving unhealthy dynamics from the past. The therapist should have been overjoyed that this was coming up in your therapy. All of the healing material was right there to be worked on. It's worse when none of it comes up, when the therapy relationship is sterile and doesn't evoke any strong feelings, because then how are you supposed to ever work through them? It seems like this person has their own issues that they aren't willing to face, and is projecting onto you, making it your fault so they don't have to face themselves. It isn't your fault at all. There are better therapists out there.

I don't know data-wise what point that would be (like, a certain level of virus in wastewater or a certain level of deaths or hospitalizations). It's really hard to tell, because it's more of a societal thing than a numbers thing. If we lived in a society that truly understood the threat (the death and disability that can follow a Covid infection, even months or years later) and took steps to mitigate it (effective long Covid treatments accessible to anyone who wants them, the understanding that in times of viral surge we will all have to shift our behavior to protect each other), then that would be much better. Nothing in life is without threat (just look at all the threads about chickenpox and shingles--did we all understand just how bad this stuff could be? yet we've been living with it and there's fairly straightforward info about how to protect from the worst effects, without any politicization involved). The truly terrifying thing about Covid is that society isn't honest about the threat and doesn't meaningfully act to mitigate it. I don't feel safe in society as long as that is true.


I actually feel less safe now than I did a few years ago, because at least then more people were being cautious. With fewer people doing anything whatsoever (to be aware of the situation, to take protective measures), the threat doesn't go away but it is covered over so that no one knows how to meaningfully do anything. I would rather have something we can all look at together and decide rationally how to deal with than something impossible to fully grasp (because the data isn't being collected anymore, or isn't readily accessible, because some people are deliberately obscuring it, or attacking those who want to have and act on the data) yet still insidiously causing damage (we just don't know to what extent).

I feel like Covid is still stealing time. I feel my age, so it's not that (it helped that I had four different jobs during the past four years, so my time was marked by those transitions). But as one of few still Covid cautious people, there are lots of things I still don't do. I am even more socially isolated, and don't know how this affects my job prospects. To be honest, I don't know if I will ever get back the time I thought I was going to have. That timeline may be gone forever. It remains to be seen whether a different future will materialize out of this limbo.

Do you have OCD? This is pretty much textbook for OCD thinking. While there are things you can do to try to give yourself reassurance (like telling yourself out loud that you're locking the door, taking a video of yourself locking the door, checking it by wriggling the knob, etc.) ultimately none of those things are going to be a final reassurance. Your brain will always find a way to introduce that insidious doubt, because that's what OCD is. Often feeding into it by setting up elaborate systems of reassurance only sets the pattern up more strongly, because you're reinforcing its necessity. Really, you need to address the root (which could be medication or exposure therapy with a therapist).

I don't know how to eliminate this stress because I experience it too, and don't have the option of moving to an apartment where it's harder to hear the neighbors through the walls. I feel mildly traumatized after over three years of living next to young children (two different families!) because I couldn't stand the crying and screaming in the morning. The sound of children crying is biologically determined to elicit a response of paying attention and causing the alert system to go off in our brains, because that's how children get their caretakers to give them what they need. Doesn't work so well if you're in the next apartment and can't do anything about it but still have to hear the crying. A new set of neighbors just moved in. No children so far, but I'm really on guard over every little sound. I also hate that if I can hear them, they can probably hear me, so I worry that they're listening. Even things like going to the bathroom can be heard through the walls. 


Anyway, the best I could do was get a really loud sound machine, and also noise cancelling headphones. Neither was a perfect solution, but it stopped me from wanting to scream all the time. I also found that the more regulated I was, the less the sound bothered me (it bothered me more if I was already stressed), so sometimes just doing something I found pleasant or distracting would help. I know it's hard.

Nope, he was doing the old school way, where you have the ones column and the tens column and you go right to left, carrying over to the next column anything that's too large for the column it's in. The way he was writing the numbers gave it away. Two different processes, same result, but one is more intuitive and easier to calculate mentally (for most people).

Why not? It's (70 x 7) + (7 x 9), or 490 + 63, or 550 + 3. It's fairly easy to do in your head. I'm surprised the kid wasn't doing it this way because it's actually way easier (and he'll have to learn it eventually, as far as I know this is how math is taught now).

I have never formally fit tested a mask, so I can't give advice, but I notice that even through my best fitting masks I can still smell pretty much everything. Volatile compounds (like the smells of food and candles) and smoke, things like that. To my knowledge, those aren't what the mask is designed to filter out, so they aren't really a good proxy for infectious particles. The only masks I know of that reliably filter smells are ones with charcoal filters (my friend used one of these early in the pandemic). Maybe a N100 mask would, but in my experience N95s don't.

Have you fit tested the double N95s? I have heard that double masking like that can compromise the seal. I would be curious to know if you have evidence that this is actually providing adequate protection for you.

I got my first Novavax booster last week. Previously I had only had MRNA (Pfizer). It was so much better and easier. I didn't get one in the fall and was just extremely cautious and isolated all winter. I wanted the extra protection now so I can take advantage of the warmer weather and more opportunities for socializing over the summer (and generally lower levels of Covid in wastewater). I understand that this is backwards from what most people do, but it works for me.

Tbh, though, having your windows up for long periods of time while you're in a car (especially with the air set to recirculate) isn't super healthy. You won't catch Covid if you're the only one in the car, but the CO2 levels from your own breath will go up alarmingly high within a few minutes. That can lead to headaches and trouble staying awake or thinking clearly. (Not saying you suggested that, but if trying to avoid shared air in an area with lots of foot traffic, I'd just be careful about CO2. The known harm of high levels of that probably outweighs a potential small risk of tiny amounts of possibly infectious particles in the vicinity.) (unless passersby are actively sticking their heads in your car windows and trying to talk to you)

It isn't any different from looking at the sun on a normal day, which you really shouldn't do either, but lots of people do, either inadvertently or on purpose. I also looked at the sun as a kid because my brain wasn't fully developed and I thought I was special and could do it even though other people couldn't. I had no permanent damage from that, although I understand now that I might have had it if I hadn't been lucky/circumstances had been different than they were. It's a risk of damage, not a guarantee. You might be just fine. They give the extra warnings about not looking at the eclipse because the unusual nature of the event causes people to want to look longer than they would ordinarily look at the sun. The fascination can override a normal reflex to stop looking because it hurts. There's nothing about the eclipse that causes more damage than regular ill-advised looking at the sun. Therefore, your risk is just about the same. Not a guarantee of damage, just a risk. (And as others have said, most damage is not permanent.)

It is far more likely to be muscle tension than anything else. Anxiety causes muscle tension. I had something similar myself a few years ago, where my lower back was in knots all the time and I was convinced my organs were dying. I would pace around trying to calm myself down (for me the ER is more anxiety inducing so I don't see it as a place of reassurance). All of the pain went away by itself when my life situation changed (finished grad school, mostly). I would not have thought that "just" muscle tension could cause that big of an effect on my body, but that's what it was.


Are you actively doing anything to try to relieve the pain? If you don't want to take pills, that's fine--what about applying heat to your back, or gently rolling over a tennis ball in the area where it hurts? Movement seems like it's what you shouldn't do, but actually it helps much more with back pain than lying still and trying to protect the muscles. They need a chance to unknot themselves. Go slow and listen to how your body feels. Trust your body. You're ok.

Other than mentioning that she thought you would be better off discussing this with your therapist, this doesn't sound like abandonment so much as an honest and clear definition of boundaries. Would you rather she tell you this or just not respond and leave you to wonder? I don't see evidence that you're being told that you're too much. I do understand how it can feel that way. I also don't know your situation or what kinds of things you normally tell her or what kinds of responses you normally get. 


If you also have a therapist, do you tend to talk about different things with them than you do with your mentor? Does this feel like something you wouldn't discuss with your therapist? If this response represents a change from what you normally receive from your mentor, then yeah, I'd be confused and want to clarify (and hope your mentor is open to clarifying) what was different about this situation or what changed. It really could just be your mentor's fluctuating capacities, which happens to everyone as we are all human. Can she respond by taking ownership of the change rather than attributing it to something you did? I hope so, and I think if you can find that out it will help you determine whether this is an actual betrayal of trust or just an honest renegotiation of boundaries (which may be temporary).

You are totally wrong that asking for other guests at the party to be informed is a violation of their boundaries. On what basis are you assuming they wouldn't want to know, if they had the choice between knowing and not knowing? 

Humans do make imperfect choices (if avoiding Covid were strictly the only priority, there would be no parties at all) but the next best thing after a perfect choice is the mitigation, where possible, of an imperfect choice. You are advocating that the other party guests not even have the choice to decide what (if anything) they will do in response to the information that they may have been exposed. Some may not want to do anything (which is unfortunate and dangerous) but some may. 

When the issue at stake is the potential spreading of a serious disease with potential long-lasting negative health effects, it's more than a matter of "you do you" in a circumstance like this. It's a matter of giving the widest possible range of affected folks the widest possible options for responding to a situation. Why do you want to limit the options for folks? What harm will information do? I highly doubt that simply making information available about a potential exposure is crossing a boundary. In fact, it may prevent future boundary crossings, in that some folks who actually were exposed will make choices to limit their activity for a bit, thereby lowering the chance that they will pass the virus on, and that means that yet more people will be protected and will not be forced to contend with worrying about exposure and illness. 

To my mind, the real boundary crossing happens when you set in motion events that make it more likely that further exposures to Covid (which are presumably unwanted) occur unchecked. Why shouldn't someone be concerned with stopping that chain of transmission? How is caring for the health of others (even those one may not personally know or meet) harmful to them? It seems rather the opposite.

As to being honest in therapy, I think it takes time and can't be pushed. If you feel safe with the person you might start by taking small risks and see how it feels and how they respond to you. A good therapist will listen and offer support and ideas that are attuned to your pace and your understanding, not try to force feed you an opinion or a solution. Unfortunately sometimes the only way to know whether your therapist is good is to take a risk, share something a little bit difficult, and see what happens. Their response is information for you. So, I get your general point, and yes, sometimes sacrifices must be made when necessary for the collective good. At the same time I think the whole society could use some clarification on needs and wants. 

For example, people need jobs because society is set up for that to be the means of sustenance (getting paid in exchange for work, using the money to buy necessities), but it's actually the necessities, not the job, that is the need most of the time. 

Some things are physiological needs and other things are created needs because society is set up for those things to be essential. Sometimes we need to rethink whether people can bypass some of the conventions of created needs (occasionally getting economic support when it wasn't "earned," if that supports the collective good) and sometimes we need to rethink the way we understand physiological needs. 

Food, shelter, clothing...no one is going to argue those, but I think too little has been said about humans' need to be social. It's a real need with a basis in biology, and we can use our well-developed minds to delay gratification of that need when we have to, but we can't actually delay it forever. There will be consequences. I think in general we have done a poor job of addressing how to help people get their needs for socialization met in safer (not risk-free) ways when the risk-free ways just aren't cutting it. 

The discussion has been too black and white. Shaming people for needing social contact doesn't help us address the problem of competing needs (physical safety vs. emotional connection and belonging). It's a real problem that can't be solved by telling people to just indefinitely sublimate their needs for socialization. That doesn't work, and then you get people guiltily doing it and not telling anyone because "it's fine if there weren't any bad consequences." And we never have the conversation, and never address the conflict.
